stories.topic: How Hoover's Tariff Blunder Handed Trump His Power
stories.summary: Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tariffs into law in 1930 even though thousands of economists and academics urged him not to. The US raised tariffs on the rich countries, they retaliated, and world trade fell 66%. Hoover lost the election. Roosevelt then asked Congress for presidential authority on trade, through the RTAA of 1934, so the president could negotiate reciprocal tariff cuts. That authority still exists today.
stories.insight: An institution built to undo one tariff disaster became the lever for the next one. Trump can impose sweeping tariffs on his own because of a power Congress handed the president to bring tariffs down. Amit adds that the trade war cut world trade by as much as you would expect from a world war.
stories.quote: And Roosevelt went to the Congress and asked for presidential authority on trade, authority that persists still today. That's how Donald Trump has so much power.

stories.topic: Pakistan's Outrage Over India Being Its 'Most Favoured Nation'
stories.summary: In trade treaties, 'most favoured nation' (MFN) means that a tariff cut negotiated with one country is extended to every country. Ajay recalls amused commentary in the Pakistani press about hawks who were outraged that Pakistan treats India as its 'most favoured nation'. They read a piece of trade plumbing as a statement of friendship.
stories.insight: Technical jargon read through a nationalist lens can turn into political outrage. In trade, MFN is not a compliment. It is a non-discrimination rule that pushes every country's tariffs down.
stories.quote: And many hawks in Pakistan are outraged that how can you treat India as your most favored nation?

stories.topic: Leopard Tanks to Ukraine, Machine Tools to Russia
stories.summary: Germany was sending Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine. At the same time the question arose whether Germany should keep selling Russia the precision machine tools used to make the T-90 tanks on the other side. That contradiction made pure free-trade positions hard to hold and pushed governments toward export controls on military and dual-use goods.
stories.insight: Trade and war are not two separate worlds. Once a real conflict exists, the free-trade logic of 'sell to whoever pays' collides with the logic of not arming your enemy. Dual-use technology makes the line very messy.
stories.quote: Why would you arm the people who are fighting wars with you?

stories.topic: India's Pharma Industry and the Chinese API Lever
stories.summary: India makes good-quality generic drugs for the world, but many of the raw ingredients (APIs) are imported from China. About 80% of the world's API capacity sits in China. Ideally an Indian firm like Dr. Reddy's buying from a Chinese supplier is a private-to-private deal. But Chinese firms are indirectly controlled by the Communist Party, so Ajay imagines a negotiation over Ladakh in which China threatens in private to cut off API exports. Ajay, Vijay Kelkar and co-authors have worked on how India could reduce this vulnerability with minimal, uncorrupt state intervention. He says the daft way would be to hand one company at a time a big contract.
stories.insight: Specialisation is the source of gains from trade, but a chokepoint held by a hostile state becomes a weapon. For every threat that is carried out publicly, there are likely many more made behind closed doors.
stories.quote: These kinds of things would be threatened in closed rooms because when you have a vulnerability that turns into the power to threaten a government.

stories.topic: Rare Earths: A Monopoly Built on Tolerating Pollution
stories.summary: Rare-earth deposits are not unique to China; they exist everywhere. Producing them is painful and polluting, and China's lax pollution regulation let it become a global monopoly. China blocked rare-earth sales to Japan around 2011. Days before this recording it announced a blockage of sales, which Ajay also describes as aimed at the United States. The processing is not inherently hard, but the knowledge would take years to rebuild elsewhere.
stories.insight: A monopoly can come from being willing to absorb a cost that others refuse, not from innovation. Once the know-how is gone from the rest of the world, the holder gains leverage that lasts for years.
stories.quote: It's not like the natural resources are unique to China, the natural resources are everywhere. It's just that it's a painful thing to make and it involves a lot of pollution.

stories.topic: The Grapes of Nashik and Europe's Pesticide Rules
stories.summary: On a visit to Sahyadri Farms, a farmer-connected organisation in Nashik, Ajay and Amit learned that grapes exported to Europe face strict phytosanitary rules. For example, no pesticides can be used for two months before harvest. Indian exporters have had to build entire supply chains around such practices.
stories.insight: A strict standard is not automatically a trade barrier. If French and Indian growers face the same rule, it is a level playing field, and a democracy has the right to choose its own safety standards.
stories.quote: Now that's a level playing field whether you grow grapes in France or you grow grapes in Nashik. It's the same rules.

stories.topic: Apple's iPhone Airlift Out of Madras
stories.summary: As the Trump tariffs on China landed, newspapers reported that Apple was filling planes 'to the gills' with iPhones and flying them from Madras to America. Shipping from China to America no longer made sense under the new tariffs.
stories.insight: It is a vivid picture of the uncertainty shock. Supply chains optimised over decades get rewired overnight, and large companies spend effort routing around policy whims instead of producing.
stories.quote: We saw newspaper stories of Apple filling up planes to the gills with very large numbers of iPhones and shipping them out of Madras to America because transporting from China to America just made no sense with the new tariffs.

stories.topic: India's Olive Branch: Dropping the Google Tax
stories.summary: When the tariff trouble began, the Indian government on its own initiative removed the 6% 'equalisation levy', popularly called the Google tax. In effect it was saying it understood that such measures are not considered good behaviour in the new world of trade.
stories.insight: A smart negotiating move is to give up your own bad policies as concessions. They cost the country nothing it should value, and they build goodwill.
stories.quote: the Indian side proactively put out an olive branch by removing the so-called six percent equalization levy, the Google tax, which I always thought was a dumb idea.

stories.topic: When a Used Car Cost More Than a New One
stories.summary: Amit recalls 1980s India, when a second-hand car cost more than a new one because a new car took seven years to be delivered. A telephone connection also meant a seven-year wait, and everything was expensive even for the elite. The 1991 opening-up ended that world. He argues that removing today's tariffs and non-tariff barriers would make cars about 30% cheaper: the car he bought for ten lakhs would have cost seven.
stories.insight: People normalise the costs of protectionism and stop seeing them. Recalling how absurd the licence-raj world was shows how much hidden cost today's tariffs still impose.
stories.quote: we had normalized that world where a secondhand car would cost more than a new car. Because a new car would take seven years to get delivered.

stories.topic: Weeping Over Adolescence in Business Class
stories.summary: Flying back from Spain on Etihad business class, Amit watched Adolescence on his iPad. He first suspected the one-take-per-episode format was a gimmick, but within minutes decided it was essential, because with no cuts, your attention never cuts either. By the first half of the fourth episode he was weeping on the flight, while nearby passengers looked at him as if to ask how one of the luckiest people around could be crying.
stories.insight: Great craft in a mainstream, hugely popular show can still overwhelm you. Amit uses this as evidence against the idea that popular culture is in decline.
stories.quote: In terms of storytelling craft, in terms of the way it was shot, in terms of the acting, I have never seen something so good. That I was weeping in the flight.

stories.topic: Kemi Badenoch Grilled for Not Watching Netflix
stories.summary: Through a tweet by Andrew Doyle, Amit found a British breakfast-TV interview in which two anchors harangued opposition leader Kemi Badenoch for not having watched Adolescence. She said she had been travelling the country talking to parents and children, and that understanding what is wrong with hospitals does not require watching Casualty. The female anchor called the show 'a great documentary', though it is fiction, which suggested the anchors had not watched it either.
stories.insight: A work of art turns into a political litmus test, wielded by people who have not engaged with it. Amit argues the show is about the human condition, not any political agenda.
stories.quote: to understand what is wrong with hospitals, for example, I don't need to watch Casualty.

recommendations.item: Adolescence
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation of the episode. It is a four-episode Netflix series, each episode shot in a single take, which he watched on a flight back from Spain.
recommendations.reason: The one-take format makes the action unfold organically and holds your attention without a break. He calls it a new pinnacle in filmmaking and is amazed that something this good is also this popular. He says to ignore the political spin from both right and left, because it is about the human condition.

recommendations.item: Dekalog
recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
recommendations.context: Recommended by Amit in an earlier episode and brought up again here as his benchmark while praising Adolescence.
recommendations.reason: Ten films made for Polish television, which he calls 'a web series before the web'. He thought it was the pinnacle of cinema and had never seen anything like it.

recommendations.item: The Wire
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the series that set a new high mark for Amit once web series arrived.
recommendations.reason: It brought a novelistic ethic to the screen, with events unfolding organically and with the sweep of a great novel.

recommendations.item: Anora
recommendations.context: Cited as this year's Oscar winner for Best Film, as part of Amit's argument that we live in a golden age of cinema.
recommendations.reason: He says the last 20 to 25 minutes are 'so masterful'. Its win shows that great films now take the Oscar, where a couple of decades ago the award often went to mainstream pap.

recommendations.item: Perfect Days
recommendations.context: Part of Amit's list of things Ajay should watch to engage with contemporary culture.
recommendations.reason: Amit's position is that engaging with films like this is engaging with the humanities: culture, life, and understanding human beings.

recommendations.item: Want Free Trade? May I Introduce You to the Tariff
recommendations.creator: Robert Lighthizer
recommendations.context: A New York Times column of 6 February 2025, which Ajay uses to steelman the Trumpist case. He reads aloud its list of government subsidies, market access limits, rigged health and safety standards, directed banking, currency manipulation and predatory tax systems.
recommendations.reason: It was the best piece he found from the American right. Several people sent it to him asking how he would respond, and writing a thorough rebuttal forced him to sharpen his thinking. He says to read it for its cleanest arguments and ignore the many bad ones.

recommendations.item: Andrew Doyle's tweet on Kemi Badenoch's grilling
recommendations.creator: Andrew Doyle
recommendations.context: The tweet through which Amit discovered the breakfast-TV interview in which Kemi Badenoch was harangued for not watching Adolescence.
recommendations.reason: Amit likes Doyle a lot and calls him a great free-speech thinker. The clip shows how a show gets turned into a political cudgel.

recommendations.item: Envisioning an India-US free trade agreement
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A Business Standard piece Ajay wrote after the Emerging Markets Conference of December 2024, cited in the chapter on India's opportunity.
recommendations.reason: It records a striking consensus on the American side that a deep free trade agreement with India is one of the few politically feasible things in the US. Ajay thinks the argument matters even more now that tariff fights have begun.

recommendations.item: India's supply chain vulnerability with Chinese APIs
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and others
recommendations.context: Linked to Ajay's account of the design he, Vijay Kelkar and co-authors worked out for reducing Indian pharma's dependence on Chinese APIs. It was originally a book chapter on the India-China relationship and later published as a blog piece.
recommendations.reason: It shows how to pursue supply-chain security in a sophisticated, uncorrupt way with minimal state intervention, instead of the daft approach of handing one company at a time a big contract.

recommendations.item: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's discussion of the problems China poses for free trade.
recommendations.reason: It is the written companion to the episode's most uncomfortable argument: why a committed free trader worries about a systemically important, rule-breaking revisionist power.

recommendations.item: Where did the Bombay Club go wrong?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It pairs with Amit's point about the Bombay Club, the group of industrialists who wanted state control of the economy.
recommendations.reason: It is background on why some industrialists choose protection over competing in a global market.

recommendations.item: Trade liberalisation: Looking beyond the WTO
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the discussion of why the WTO model ran out of steam.
recommendations.reason: It supports the episode's case that the way forward is deep integration among willing countries rather than another simple multilateral round.

recommendations.item: Egregious Indian protectionism against trade in services
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It connects to Ajay's points that services now dominate world GDP and that India runs non-tariff barriers such as data localisation.
recommendations.reason: It applies the services-trade argument to India's own barriers.

recommendations.item: India: An agricultural trade powerhouse
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It connects to Ajay's remark that the GATT abandoned agriculture, even though more free trade in agriculture is in India's interest.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case for India's stake in agricultural trade.

recommendations.item: Two divergent measures
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes, with a URL pointing to an uncertainty piece. It sits next to Ajay's argument that the Trump tariffs are above all an uncertainty shock to the world economy.
recommendations.reason: It is further reading on the uncertainty dimension of the current moment.

recommendations.item: Implications of US tariffs
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the chapter on the Trump tariffs.
recommendations.reason: It is Ajay's written take on what the tariffs mean, as a companion to the episode's discussion.

recommendations.item: The Globalisation Episode (Episode 95 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous week's episode, which this one continues.
recommendations.reason: It covers the 101: first principles of globalisation, why tariffs are terrible, and a potted intellectual history up to World War II. It is the foundation this episode builds on.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Plugged by Amit when Ajay explains that the GATT left out agriculture.
recommendations.reason: It gives a comprehensive picture of what ails Indian agriculture, where 40 to 60% of people work in the sector, compared with about 5% in the developed world.

recommendations.item: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to 'our clean energy episodes' while discussing polysilicon and solar panels.
recommendations.reason: It is background for the example of China building scale-driven, subsidised dominance in simple products like solar panels.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Invoked by Ajay ('like we say in the development episode') when explaining why lost manufacturing know-how is hard to rebuild.
recommendations.reason: It develops the idea that development is learning by doing, not following a manual.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's closing note that deep trade liberalisation now would 'please the soul of Manmohan Singh' and the other reformers.
recommendations.reason: It covers the reformers whose 1991 opening-up is the model for the opportunity India now has.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay frames the trade debate as a choice between two outlooks. The martial outlook grabs land; the shopkeeper's outlook trades its way to whatever it wants. When countries are shut out of trade, as after Smoot-Hawley, they turn to armies and territory, from Japan's 1931 invasion to Italy's conquest of Ethiopia and German Lebensraum. Amit adds that this is not a binary: the positive-sum world of trade will always coexist with, and be shaped by, the negative-sum world of war.
core_ideas.quote: Every push in favor of autarky is taking us closer to a military and a martial outlook and a way to make progress by killing people.

core_ideas.explanation: Britain grew rich by cutting tariffs unilaterally, which is pure Ricardian logic. The US political bargain of 1934 was different: the president could cut tariffs when other countries cut theirs too. Built into that law was most-favoured-nation treatment, meaning a cut negotiated with one country applies to all. That avoids a messy patchwork of country-specific rates and goods being routed through third countries, and it creates a steady bias toward lower tariffs everywhere. Amit's gloss is that you treat everyone the way you treat your best friend.
core_ideas.quote: It was a simple idea that whatever you're going to do, you do for everybody.

core_ideas.concept: Why the GATT Worked, and Why It Stopped Working
core_ideas.explanation: The GATT succeeded because its designers left out agriculture to avoid fights with small but lethal farm lobbies, trade in 1945 meant manufactured goods, global corporations lobbied for liberalisation, and the West used military and aid leverage to bring spoilers like India along. Each piece later broke down. Services are now about 67% of GDP in the median country (71.5% for the OECD) and barely covered by trade rules. Corporations lost interest once their goods agenda was done. Elites assumed the battle was won. After the Cold War the West cut its military, foreign-policy and aid budgets, losing leverage in a WTO where any 'dinky country' can veto. Ajay would even trade away some manufacturing for sweeping free trade in services.
core_ideas.quote: So really it's game over. You move to services. Why hanker after manufacturing?

core_ideas.concept: The Gain From Trade Is the Imports
core_ideas.explanation: The benefit of trade is being able to buy cheap things from abroad, not exporting. India sells software and uses the money to buy cheap solar panels; if the Chinese state subsidises those panels, that is a gift to Indian consumers. Amit pushes this through Smith and Ricardo: when cheap goods close local factories, consumers save money, and that money creates economic activity and jobs elsewhere. If someone subsidises us, we should take the subsidy with open arms.
core_ideas.quote: The privilege of international trade does not come from exporting. The privilege of international trade comes from the glory of being able to buy cheap things from overseas.

core_ideas.concept: Four Reasons Even a Free Trader Worries
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's four doubts about free trade are these. (1) Military conflict: selling capabilities to an enemy, and losing your own industrial base. (2) Economic statecraft: specialisation creates chokepoints, such as APIs and rare earths, that a hostile state can squeeze. (3) Hidden subsidies plus economies of scale: cheap directed credit, expropriated land and subsidised inputs let Chinese firms dominate products like polysilicon and solar panels and set them up for monopoly pricing later. (4) Macroeconomic dumping: a large economy that answers its own debt overhang by flooding the world with cheap goods exports its unemployment. He also sets himself a rule: anyone raising such worries must spell out concrete scenarios of harm.
core_ideas.quote: A person like me who is getting worried about this must explicitly articulate scenarios of harm. And specific examples of harm. Otherwise, it's incoherent.

core_ideas.concept: Military Strength Lives in the Civilian Economy
core_ideas.explanation: Modern defence economics stresses the military industrial base. A country with a commercial shipbuilding industry can repurpose it to build warships; one without it cannot. In World War II the US was 'the arsenal of democracy' because it was the world's greatest manufacturer, but that capability now sits in China. Requiring 'Made in India' for military procurement does not work if the wider private economy lacks the skills.
core_ideas.quote: It doesn't work to just say I will have a little vertical isolated island of private firms who make for military applications, while the rest of the private sector simply doesn't have these capabilities.

core_ideas.explanation: Free trade assumes partners who will not turn dependence into a weapon. Depending on Britain for APIs would be fine, because Britain is a status-quo power with a good relationship with India. China is a one-party state, a 'party that has a country', with a century-of-humiliation grievance and wolf-warrior diplomacy. Ajay names China and Russia as revisionist powers that are hostile to the liberal order. The ideal is a system of alliances in which countries credibly promise never to do such things to each other, so that trade can work as Ricardo described.
core_ideas.quote: Like between India and the UK, this would never happen.

core_ideas.concept: Manufacturing Know-How Is Hard to Rebuild
core_ideas.explanation: Complex manufacturing is not a book you can copy. Ajay calls this learning by doing that takes years to build. When subsidised Chinese firms hollow out production elsewhere, the knowledge disappears, and a supply cutoff becomes very disruptive. He also calls this a breach of faith: China was admitted to the WTO on the understanding it would play by the rules, and its hidden subsidies have drained political support for free trade among lawmakers and academics.
core_ideas.quote: That economic development is not a manual, it's learning by doing. It takes years and years for each country to develop those skills.

core_ideas.explanation: Textbooks say a firm cuts prices to kill rivals and then raises them once it has a monopoly. Amit calls this rubbish: Amazon, Jio and cell-phone firms never did it, and it only happens with state coercion. Ajay reframes the question as how contestable the industry is, not whether a monopoly exists. If Amazon overcharged for hand towels, Myntra would step in. Rebuilding a complex manufacturing supply chain would take five to ten years. He adds that a $19-trillion single-party state with no checks and balances is a new situation. The two did not resolve this and suggested a future episode on monopolies.
core_ideas.quote: Give me an example where without the coercive power of the state coming into play, a company has first taken a monopoly by lowering prices and then raised them.

core_ideas.concept: Not Every Regulation Is a Trade Barrier
core_ideas.explanation: Lighthizer counts strict standards, low taxes and weak regulation as unfair trade practices. Ajay separates the two cases. Rules that apply equally to local and foreign firms, like GDPR or Europe's rules for grapes, are a democracy's birthright. Each country also chooses its own trade-off on local pollution, labour rules and taxation, so India's lower standards are not a subsidy. Carbon dioxide is the exception, because it is a global pollutant. Real non-tariff barriers do exist, such as India's data-localisation rules, which keep out good foreign cloud providers and raise costs for Indians. Some of the critique holds up, and some is mumbo jumbo.
core_ideas.quote: You can't take today's Swedish standard and apply that to India.

core_ideas.explanation: Trump treats a country's bilateral trade deficit as a measure of its non-tariff barriers, and his team even derived tariff rates from it. The idea Ajay attributes to Amit makes the point: you run a deficit with your egg seller because you buy his eggs and he never buys your podcasting services. Specialisation naturally produces bilateral imbalances.
core_ideas.quote: it's like this is nonsense to think that country by country you should look at the bilateral trade deficit.

core_ideas.explanation: The bigger harm is unpredictability, not any single tariff. If the US can do this, firms wonder what it might do next. Every firm planning its next factory faces a headache, and the supply chains built over decades, with a factory in Madras, another in China, another in Argentina and distribution in America, are thrown into disarray. Amit adds that uncertainty distorts investment, planning and expansion.
core_ideas.quote: Intuitively, the destruction of this global arrangement is tantamount to throwing bombs on certain present production facilities. So it's like reducing the capital stock of the world.

core_ideas.concept: Deep Integration: A WTO 2.0 With Open Architecture
core_ideas.explanation: The way forward is a group of willing countries negotiating deep liberalisation that covers subsidies, directed banking, currency manipulation, IP theft, carbon and treatment of foreign firms, so tightly that cheating is hard. The Trans-Pacific Partnership was conceived this way. Because the Chinese Communist Party is a concern and the US has lost capability, Ajay would leave both out and build the core from the rest of the OECD plus India. Others like Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Pakistan could join later on take-it-or-leave-it terms.
core_ideas.quote: But now we are here. We've got many years of experience, and now we need to think of deep integration.

core_ideas.concept: India's Opportunity in the Tariff Crisis
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sees a deep India-US free trade agreement as feasible and urgent. Trump could claim he opened fifteen closed doors, India could say it secured a deal with a key partner, and similar deals could follow with the UK, EU and Japan. He praises the Union government's thinking here. Amit goes further and wants India to remove all tariffs unilaterally, for all countries. Ajay adds that non-tariff barriers must go too. The payoff would be cars about 30% cheaper and better, cheaper goods across the board.
core_ideas.quote: my dream is that we have no tariffs at all. Forget trade agreements, unilaterally remove all tariffs, get rid of tariff barriers, it will help our people.

core_ideas.explanation: Business can respond to liberalisation in two ways. It can ask for protection and rule a small, fixed pond, as the Bombay Club did when it backed state control of the Indian economy. Or it can demand a global market and grow into great companies by competing, as firms in the developed world did when they lobbied for the GATT.
core_ideas.quote: protect us from the global market, we will rule in our small pond of a fixed size.

core_ideas.concept: Progress Must Be Won Anew Each Generation
core_ideas.explanation: Elites repeatedly assumed the argument was settled: the 1909 book that said trade had made war obsolete, Fukuyama's End of History, and the Washington Consensus formula for development. Popular opposition never went away. The case for open trade has to be argued again by every generation, and some generations did not try hard enough.
core_ideas.quote: It was a battle that every generation had to fight anew, and one can say that some generations didn't try hard enough to fight it anew.

core_ideas.explanation: Steelmanning is the opposite of a straw man: you state your opponent's argument so well that they could have said it themselves, and only then disagree. Amit demonstrates it by restating Ajay's case about China before setting out his own dissent from Smith and Ricardo.
core_ideas.quote: To steel man is to express their argument so well that they could have done it themselves in that way.

core_ideas.concept: Engage With Culture Before Dismissing It
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues we are in a golden age of cinema and culture. Masterpieces like Adolescence are hugely popular, and films like Anora now win the Oscar. He challenges Ajay, who often says popular culture is dumbing down, to engage with it first, because culture is part of the humanities Ajay always urges people to study.
core_ideas.quote: This is the humanities. It's not just studying history and sociology. It's culture. This is life, understanding human beings.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on his bad hair day: 'When I started The Seen and the Unseen... they would ask me why an audio podcast and I would say I have a face for audio. I have realized today... I also have a head for audio.' He also describes washing his hair and then working to make it look 'naturally uncombed'.

Amit on the tariff formula: one of the officials who published the math had an Indian name, and someone on Twitter joked, 'just imagine they hired the one Indian who doesn't know math.' Amit adds: 'If you're watching this, learn some math, bro. While you're working for Trump.'

Ajay, recalling Amit's favourite illustration of why bilateral deficits are meaningless: 'I have a bilateral trade deficit with my local shop that sells me eggs because I only buy eggs from him and he never buys the services of a prominent podcaster.'
Ajay on the tariff rollout: 'Into this came a stable genius called Donald Trump.' After Trump started exempting phones and CPUs, he says: 'this is everything but a stable genius.'
Ajay on the poor preparation behind the tariffs: 'there is no tariff on Russia, and there are tariffs on countries that have no people.'

Ajay points out the irony: he had worried about the Chinese Communist Party cutting off goods to the world, 'Well, here you've got the Republican Party blocking the sale of those Chinese things into America.'

After Ajay describes 'cost complexity fear that is going to turn into an adverse global macroeconomic shock', Amit translates: 'You used a lot of jargon there. What you actually meant to say is that the shit has hit the fan.'

When Ajay calls 1989 'one of the great achievements of human history', Amit quickly clarifies: 'You mean to say the collapse was one of the great achievements, in case anyone misunderstands not the USSR.' Ajay says it was one of the happiest moments of his life.

Amit on Indian politics: 'All parties are... left wing on economics, right wing on society, which is exactly the opposite of what it should be, because they're both anti-freedom.' He adds that Trump and Bernie Sanders are similar in their anti-free-trade thinking. Ajay says the whole left-right vocabulary has 'become a khichdi'.
Ajay on Japan's farm lobby: rice farmers are 'a lethal lobby', about two percent of the population, in 'the country that is making semiconductors. But why pick fights?'

Amit weeping at Adolescence in business class while nearby passengers seemed to wonder how 'one of the luckiest people ever' could be crying, adding: 'you can have all the champagne you want, though of course I never drink.'

Amit says Ajay agreed to watch an episode of Adolescence on his iPad after the shoot 'and then found a way to wriggle out', and demands 'a public commitment, Ajay Shah, that before the airing of this episode you will watch Adolescence.' Ajay commits only to episode one, and Amit concedes that four hours 'is a huge commitment.'

When Ajay says Keynes would be dreaming of a deep, open trade agreement, Amit quips, 'In the long run, Keynes is right,' a twist on Keynes's own 'in the long run' line. Ajay sighs: 'Sadly, we don't have a John Maynard Keynes today.'

Smoot-Hawley tariffs (1930): signed by Hoover despite thousands of economists objecting, they set off retaliation that cut world trade by 66%. Ajay links this to Japan's 1931 invasion, Italy's 1935 conquest of Ethiopia and the German idea of Lebensraum.

'Make love, not war': Ajay borrows the slogan for the shopkeeper's outlook. He contrasts it with Britain, the 'nation of shopkeepers' that built navies and a trading system, and says 'Britannia ruled the waves' because it unilaterally cut tariffs.
John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White, who from 1944 onwards designed the post-war order: the IMF, World Bank, Marshall Plan and GATT.
'The arsenal of democracy': the World War II phrase for America's manufacturing might, which Ajay says now sits in China.
Thomas Mun and Friedrich List, whom Amit names as classic voices of mercantilism and economic nationalism. Their arguments are a standard trope that economic thinking has repeatedly defeated.
Wolf-warrior diplomacy and China's 'century of humiliation': Ajay's shorthand for the grievances that make China a revisionist power.

The Great Illusion (1909), discussed in the previous episode, which held that widespread trade meant no more war. Also Francis Fukuyama's End of History, where Amit notes 'end' meant the means-and-ends sense and the original essay had a question mark. And the Washington Consensus, the idea that development was a solved formula. All three are cautionary tales of elite complacency.
Joan Robinson's metaphor, invoked by Amit for unilateral free trade: 'we've put rocks on our own coastline, remove the rocks.'
Europe's GDPR, which Amit cites as a commonly alleged non-tariff barrier, recalling J. D. Vance protesting it. Ajay counters that it applies equally to European and foreign firms.

Martin Amis, as recalled by Amit: 'the worst kind of criticism is when you criticize an author for not writing the book you want.' Amit uses it against critics who fault Adolescence for centring the accused boy rather than the victim.
